newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine soldiers free Japanese after gunbattle.
newsitem.headline: Philippine soldiers free Japanese after gunbattle.

text.p: Soldiers on Monday rescued a Japanese businessman after killing two of his kidnappers in a skirmish on a mountain in the southern Philippines, officials said.

Three Filipino companions of Kenichi Takayama, including a 10-year-old boy, were also rescued after a dramatic chase in heavy rains in the mountains of Sarangani island, 1,120 km (695 miles) southeast of Manila.

"Very, very good experience," a relieved Takayama told reporters after a 28-hour ordeal that began on Sunday afternoon when six suspected Moslem guerrillas seized the four from a beach resort in Glan town.
Takayama, 49, showed bruises on his legs suffered while struggling barefoot up the mountain at the orders of his captors.
Sarangani officials said they were still verifying an earlier police report that one other kidnapper had been killed in an earlier shootout with the police on Sunday.
Another Filipino on the beach was killed by the kidnappers before they took Takayama and the others away, officials said.
"The police are still chasing the rest of the kidnappers," Sarangani governor Priscilla Chiongbian said.

News of the kidnapping came as President Fidel Ramos was leaving on a trip abroad to attract investors and cast an unwelcome spotlight on violence in a country grappling with various rebel groups and a spate of kidnappings.

"I think incidents like this will affect business. It creates instability and an environment not conducive to investors," Tess Baltazar, a spokeswoman for the Citizens Action Against Crime, told Reuters.
The latest kidnapping occurred in the Philippines' troubled southern region, home to Moslem guerrillas fighting for an Islamic state in the largely Christian nation.
Moslem renegades have been blamed for more than 40 abductions since January.

The Ramos administration signed a peace deal with the mainstream Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) last September but the accord -- not recognised by at least two other rebel factions -- has failed to bring peace.
Kidnap-for-ransom has become a booming trade in the Philippines, a country dubbed "Asia's kidnapping capital" by Fortune Magazine. Police, however, say the label is unfair.

More than 500 people have benn kidnapped in the Philippines since 1995, many of them Filipino-Chinese businessmen, and ransom totalling at least 333 million pesos ($13 million) has been paid, according to statistics released by anti-crime groups.

Army Captain Noel Detoyato said the Sarangani kidnappers belonged to the Abu Sayyaf fundamentalist group, which has been blamed for a spate of bombings and other kidnappings in the region over the past three years. The group has shunned talks with Manila.
Takayama has been a resident of nearby General Santos city for 11 years, running a company that exports mangoes and other food to Japan.

Takayama was the first Japanese kidnapped in the country since January 1994 when two Filipino soldiers kidnapped a construction firm owner in Manila. He was freed after a ransom of seven million pesos was paid.
Another Japanese, Nobuyki Wakaoji, then a director at Mitsui and Co Ltd, was the victim in one of the country's biggest kidnapping cases.
Abducted in 1986, he was released months later after payment of $3 million ransom. Two Filipino masterminds of the kidnapping are now serving life terms in jail.
Widespread belief that soldiers and police protect kidnappers has discouraged Filipinos from reporting ransom demands.
Kidnappings have continued despite Ramos's order to the military last month to take over the job of hunting down the gangs from the police, saying the army had better firepower.
